name: NCV211RSQT2G
title: Bidirectional zero-drift current-shunt monitors, voltage output, -0.3 V to 26 V common mode
summary: A family of current-sense amplifiers with a fixed internal gain of 50, 100, 200 or 500 V/V that amplify the voltage across a shunt at any common-mode voltage from -0.3 V to 26 V, whatever the supply. A zero-drift input stage keeps offset to tens of microvolts, so shunts with full-scale drops near 10 mV can be used. The REF pin sets the output level for zero current, which allows unidirectional or bidirectional sensing on the high or low side. The parts run from 2.2 V to 26 V and draw 80 µA at most; NCV parts are the automotive-qualified versions.

notes: * NCV parts are AEC-Q100 qualified and PPAP capable, built under unique-site and change-control requirements for automotive use.
R3 and R4 are the internal input resistors and R1 and R2 the internal feedback and reference resistors of the gain network.
Marking on the package: device code, date code M and a Pb-free dot.

circuits.title: High-side current sensing
circuits.description: The shunt sits between the supply and the load; IN+ goes to its supply end and IN- to its load end. VS takes 2.2 V to 26 V with a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF capacitor to ground. REF goes either to a reference voltage or to ground, and the output is VOUT = ILOAD × RSHUNT × GAIN + VREF.

parts.value: REF to reference voltage or to ground
parts.note: one of the two connections is made

circuits.title: Basic unidirectional connection
circuits.description: High-side sensing of current that only flows one way. REF is grounded, so with no current the output sits within 50 mV of ground and it rises with current to within 200 mV of VS. VS is 2.2 V to 26 V, bypassed by 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF.

circuits.title: Bidirectional sensing, REF from a shunt reference
circuits.description: Current in either direction: REF is held at a mid-level by a shunt reference or Zener fed through a resistor from a supply, and the output swings above and below that level.

circuits.title: Bidirectional sensing, REF from a series reference
circuits.description: Current in either direction: a series voltage reference running from a supply drives REF directly.

circuits.title: Bidirectional sensing, REF from a buffered divider
circuits.description: Current in either direction: a resistor divider across a supply sets the mid-level and an op amp wired as a unity-gain follower (for example NCS2003 or NCS20071) drives REF; a divider used for REF needs this buffer.

parts.value: op amp, e.g. NCS2003 or NCS20071

circuits.title: Input filter
circuits.description: A 10 Ω resistor in each input lead and a 0.25 µF capacitor across IN+ and IN- form a differential low-pass filter. With a 200 µΩ shunt carrying 1 nH, the filter time constant 2 × RFILT × CFILT covers the shunt's L/R, and it also removes high-frequency noise. REF goes to a reference voltage or to ground.

circuits.title: Remote sensing with a current output
circuits.description: A 1 kΩ resistor RIOUT from OUT to REF turns the output into a current IOUT = VOUT / RIOUT (1 mA/V), which leaves by REF over a wire to a readout board. There a 1 kΩ resistor RITOV to the readout ground turns it back into a voltage, which a line receiver amplifier (for example NCS2003) passes to an ADC. The stray ground resistance between the two boards then adds little error.

where.GAIN: fixed gain of the part: 50, 100, 200 or 500 V/V

equations.name: Input filter time constant
equations.note: The filter time constant is at least the shunt's own L/R time constant.

equations.name: Input filter capacitor with 10 Ω resistors

where.IOUT: current from the REF pin to the readout board
where.VOUT: output voltage the part would give

operation.text: A zero-drift amplifier with an on-chip resistor network sets the gain; the input resistors are 20 kΩ, 10 kΩ, 5 kΩ or 2 kΩ for gains of 50, 100, 200 and 500, and the feedback and reference resistors are 1 MΩ. The inputs accept -0.3 V to 26 V common mode with any supply from 2.2 V to 26 V. Typical curves are measured on the NCS210R.

The part works on either side of the load. Only high-side sensing sees a short from the supply line to ground, and it puts no resistance in the load's ground return. On the low side the true differential input suits Kelvin or ordinary shunts and rejects common-mode noise in the ground path, and REF still sets the output offset.

VS may be the supply whose current is measured or a separate one. To detect a short that can pull the measured supply close to 0 V, use a separate supply for VS. With two supplies, either may come up first.
Ground REF. With no shunt current the output is within 50 mV of ground; current through the shunt drives it up to within 200 mV of VS.

Bias REF to a mid-level, most often half the supply or half the reference of the measuring system, and the output moves above and below that level with current direction (charging and discharging a battery, for example).

REF needs a low-impedance source: a supply rail, a shunt or series voltage reference, or a resistor divider followed by a unity-gain buffer. A divider alone is not suitable. More than VS + 0.3 V on REF forward-biases the ESD diode from REF to VS and exceeds the absolute maximum rating.
For a noisy measured current, a filter after OUT is the simplest choice, especially into a high-impedance load; any filter parts may be used there, though a buffer may be needed after it.

Filter resistors at the inputs and any mismatch between them degrade gain, CMRR and offset, the offset partly through the input bias current, so keep each at 10 Ω or less. Choose the capacitor so the filter time constant matches the shunt's L/R, or puts the pole lower; 80 nF gives about 100 kHz. The capacitor may have a small voltage rating; it needs good high-frequency behaviour, and can be made larger for more noise filtering. Below 1 mΩ the shunt inductance adds a zero, often with corners in the low hundreds of kHz, and fast spikes on the sense line can overload the input stage even above the amplifier bandwidth; only an input filter cures that.

The 10 Ω input resistors give a place to add Zener or TVS clamps: one TVS with two diodes across the inputs, or one TVS on each input. Use Zeners or unidirectional TVS diodes that clamp at no more than 30 V, with the lowest rating the system allows. A TVS with 18 V standoff commonly clamps at up to 29.2 V; higher-power TVS parts have a sharper knee, closer to their breakdown voltage.

A larger shunt gives a more accurate reading at the cost of more power lost in it. Four-terminal (Kelvin) shunts give the best accuracy, with a separate pair of terminals for the sense connections; with two-terminal shunts, lay out the sense traces as the shunt's maker recommends.

A resistor from OUT to REF makes the output a current out of REF, which carries the reading to a distant board without error from ground drops between boards. Making RITOV equal to RIOUT gives equal drops across the two. Both resistors add voltage drop in the current path; accuracy falls off when noise or ground drop between the boards passes 1 V.

There is no shutdown pin; cutting VS with a MOSFET, a load switch or a logic gate removes the quiescent current. Current still flows into the sense pins through the internal resistor network, a little over 1 MΩ in each leg. Powered, the sense pins draw the well-matched 39 µA typical bias current. The sense pins still tolerate the full rated common-mode range with VS at zero.
The UQFN10 NC pins have no internal connection; leave them open or tie them to any voltage from GND to VS.
